newsitem.title: CANADA: WIC holders to vote on wind-up proposal.
newsitem.headline: WIC holders to vote on wind-up proposal.

text.p: Shareholders at broadcaster WIC Western International Communications Ltd will vote on a proposal to dissolve the company at its annual meeting next month -- a motion the company said is doomed to fail.

WIC revealed Monday in the proxy circular for its annual meeting January 8 that New York investment firm Oppenheimer and Co Inc had acquired 320 or 0.035 percent of its voting Class A shares, enabling it to table two motions.
In a statement included in the circular, Oppenheimer described itself as "profoundly dissatisfied" with management of the company.
Oppenheimer also put forward a motion that at least one-fifth of WIC's directors be elected by both its Class A and Class B shareholders. WIC's Class B shares do not carry voting rights.

WIC said that because 99.96 percent of its voting A shareholders -- primarily members of two families -- had decided to vote against the motions, the proposals had no chance of success. In urging shareholders to vote against Oppenheimer's motions, WIC defended its efforts to enhance shareholder value. "The prospects of the corporation have never been better," it said.

The broadcaster has sought to allay shareholder concerns over its two-tier share structure that allows the founding Griffiths family of Vancouver to control the company while owning only 7.4 percent of its total equity.

The Griffiths fought off a challenge for control from the Allard family of Alberta, the company's biggest equity holder, only to face a hostile takeover bid by rival broadcaster CanWest Global Communications Corp. That bid was blocked early this year by a court ruling against CanWest's attempt to have voting rights awarded to the company's non-voting shareholders. An appeal will be heard in February.
Chief executive John Lacey in an interview acknowledged past turmoil over control at WIC. "You're right. We are a company prone to some skirmishing around the edges," he said.

But he said he was confident that strategic initiatives under way would benefit shareholders. These include market expansion for WIC's Ontario television station CHCH, its move to launch a national local multipoint communications service and efforts to buy a Montreal TV station.
Lacey said the two-tier share structure was "predominant" in Canada's communications industry. "I do not propose to make any changes" in it, he said.

Lacey, who started at WIC in November after previous chief Doug Holtby resigned, said shareholders should trust his reputation and look to his performance as chief of Scott's Hospitality Inc. He declined to give a date when evidence of WIC's improvement would be apparent.
"We're going to work hard to improve our P&L (profit and loss statement)...You've got to look at the longer term," he said.

Lacey said he did not think it was a coincidence that Oppenheimer tabled its proposals just before CanWest's appeal is due to be heard. But he said he was confident the court would reject CanWest's argument.

Lacey also denounced Oppenheimer's motions as without merit. The wind-up proposal would be extremely disadvantageous from a tax perspective and non-voting shareholders already have board representation, he said.

Oppenheimer accused WIC of acting only in the interests of a small group of shareholders and said its voting structure has been "abused." "Past offers to purchase the corporation were never adequately explored and the views of the Class B shareholders were never represented," it said.
WIC said it was only aware of one public bid -- the CanWest offer -- which it rejected in the interests of all shareholders.
An Oppenheimer official said the firm also owns a "significant" number of WIC's Class B shares. He declined further comment.
